metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices consistent with the Tallying heuristic on the critical dissociation trials (Trials 1 and 2). In these trials, one option has a higher total number of positive features (favored by Tallying) but lacks the highest-validity features (meaning WADD strongly favors the other option). Tallying will produce a metric value close to 1, whereas WADD will produce a metric value close to 0.

The experimental design pits a single high-validity feature (feature 1, validity 0.95) against multiple lower-validity features. In every trial pair, the option that possesses feature 1 is either tied or outnumbered in the total tally of winning features. Consequently, the Tallying heuristic will never deterministically prefer the option with feature 1 (it either prefers the alternative or ties). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model heavily weights feature 1 due to its high validity, frequently choosing the option that possesses it. This metric computes the overall proportion of trials where the subject chose the option having feature 1, which will be significantly higher under WADD than Tallying.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take-The-Best (TTB) model. TTB sequentially checks features in order of validity and stops at the first discriminating feature. The experimental design contains many trials where the first discriminating feature favors one option, but the sum of the remaining features strongly favors the other. TTB will consistently choose the former, resulting in a metric close to 1.0, whereas WADD will compensate and choose the latter, resulting in a metric much closer to 0.0.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses Option B on trials where Option B has a greater total number of positive features than Option A. In the specified experimental design, these trials correspond to scenarios where Option A is supported by the single most predictive discriminating cue (which Take-The-Best relies on exclusively), while Option B is supported by a larger number of less predictive cues. Consequently, TTB will deterministically choose Option A (yielding a metric value near 0), whereas a compensatory WADD model will aggregate the multiple advantages of Option B and choose it most of the time (yielding a metric value much closer to 1).

This metric evaluates the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 1 and Trial 3. In both trials, Option A has only the highest-validity cue, while Option B has multiple lower-validity cues. From Trial 1 to Trial 3, Option B gains two additional low-validity cues. The Probabilistic Strategy Selection (Mixture) model predicts a very small difference because Tallying already strongly favors Option B in Trial 1, so adding more cues to B in Trial 3 doesn't change the Tallying choice probability much (it stays near 1). The WADD model, however, integrates all cues linearly, so the two additional cues for Option B in Trial 3 significantly increase its continuous weighted sum, leading to a much larger drop in the probability of choosing Option A.

The experimental design includes critical trials where Option A wins on the most valid cue (so Take-The-Best prefers A) and both options have the same number of positive cues (so Tallying predicts a tie). As a result, the Probabilistic Strategy Selection (Mixture) model must predict Option A more often than Option B. However, the validities are chosen such that the sum of validities for Option B is strictly greater than for Option A in these exact trials. The Weighted Additive (WADD) model, which linearly combines these validities, will therefore strongly predict Option B. By computing the choice rate of Option B on these specific trials, we expect a very high value for WADD and a low value (less than 0.5) for the Mixture model, cleanly discriminating the two.

This metric isolates a critical dissociation between the Mixture model and the Accumulator model by contrasting the probability of choosing Option A in Trial 1 versus Trial 3. In Trial 1, Option A is supported by both Take-The-Best (TTB) and Tallying, meaning the Mixture model will almost always choose A. However, the Accumulator model will choose A only if its threshold is very low; otherwise, the accumulated evidence swings to Option B, leading to a choice of B. In Trial 3, TTB supports A but Tallying supports B, so the Mixture model predicts a mixed probability of choosing A (depending on the mixing weight). Conversely, for the Accumulator model, the evidence tally in Trial 3 remains strictly positive at every single step of the sequential search, guaranteeing that it will always choose Option A regardless of its threshold. Therefore, the difference P(A | Trial 1) - P(A | Trial 3) is strictly positive for the Mixture model (approx. +0.5) and strictly non-positive for the Accumulator model (ranging from 0 to -1.0).

In Trials 1 and 2, the Mixture model (bounded by Take-The-Best and Tallying) decisively predicts Option B and Option A, respectively. By contrast, the Sequential Evidence Accumulation model, when its threshold is sufficiently high (>0.95), will integrate evidence beyond the first feature and predict the exact opposite (Option A in Trial 1, Option B in Trial 2). This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the unique SEA predictions on these two critical trials, producing a value near 0 for the Mixture model and significantly higher than 0 for the SEA model.
